en: The Scripture on the Four Fearlessnesses Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court-Scattered Grandee, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial,
and Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, Subject Shi Hu, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, having attained the four fearlessnesses, turns the great wheel of Dharma amidst the great assembly, roaring like a lion with sovereign fearlessness.”
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, bowed at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined, addressed him, saying:
“What are the Tathāgata’s four fearlessnesses?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, amidst the great assembly, I spoke these words:
'The Tathāgata has attained Right and Perfect Enlightenment.'"
When this was said, the śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, Māras, Brahmās, devas, and humans all spoke together, saying:
"What has been proclaimed here is not in accordance with the teachings of the Dharma; we have never before seen or heard of such a thing."
At that time, the World-Honored One was among that assembly, free from alarm and fear, his mind abiding in peace and bliss, dwelling in fearlessness.
He further declared:
"My body is pure; all outflows have been exhausted."
When this was said, the śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, Māras, Brahmās, devas, and humans all spoke together, saying:
"What has been proclaimed here does not accord with the teachings of the Dharma; we have never before seen or heard of such a thing."
At that time, the World-Honored One was among that assembly without alarm or fear; his mind attained peace and bliss, abiding in fearlessness.
He further addressed them, saying:
"There is one obstructive defilement that can hinder the fruit of the Path. If this obstruction is extinguished, the Noble Path will manifest of itself."
When this was said, the śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, Māras, Brahmās, devas, and humans all spoke together, saying:
"What has been proclaimed here does not accord with the teachings of the Dharma; we have never before seen or heard of such a thing."
At that time, the World-Honored One remained among that assembly without alarm or fear, his mind abiding in peace and bliss, dwelling in fearlessness.
He further addressed them, saying:
"The cultivation of morality, meditative concentration, and so forth, can bring about transcendence from birth and death, exhausting all retributions of suffering."
When this was said, the śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, Māras, Brahmās, devas, and humans all spoke together, saying:
"What has been proclaimed here does not accord with the teachings of the Dharma; we have never before seen or heard of such a thing."
At that time, the World-Honored One was among that assembly without alarm or fear; his mind attained peace and bliss, abiding in fearlessness.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This is called the Tathāgata’s turning of the Great Wheel of Dharma through the four kinds of fearlessness."
"Furthermore, monks! Among the eight great assemblies, one is fully endowed with the four fearlessnesses. What are these eight?
[The text continues as follows...]"
Once, in a certain place, there was a multitude of countless hundreds of śramaṇas—some standing, some walking, some sitting—who said to one another:
"In the past, the Buddha taught such characteristics of the Dharma as these; they are extremely profound and difficult to understand, never before seen or heard."
"Is this right or wrong?
Is it false or true?
At that time, having heard those words, the Tathāgata felt no fear or trepidation; his hair did not stand on end, and he remained sovereign and fearless, as immovable as a mountain.

Furthermore, there were countless hundreds of assemblies of brahmins, countless hundreds of assemblies of kṣatriyas, countless hundreds of assemblies of householders, countless hundreds of assemblies of the Four Great Kings, countless hundreds of assemblies of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, countless hundreds of assemblies of Māra kings, and countless hundreds of assemblies of Brahmā gods.
Thus, these eight groups of people—whether standing, or staying still, or walking, or sitting—said to one another:
"In the past, the Buddha taught such characteristics of the Dharma; they are profoundly deep and difficult to understand, never before seen or heard."
"Is this right or wrong?
Is it false or true?
At that time, having heard those words, the Tathāgata felt no fear or trepidation; his hair did not stand on end, and he remained sovereign and fearless, as immovable as a mountain.
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus! This is called attaining fearlessness among the eightfold assembly."
He then spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata, with sovereign power, turns the wheel of Dharma; In the past, he was able to accomplish the four fearlessnesses.
When gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, and śramaṇas Hear the Teacher’s words and phrases, they harbor doubts.”

With body and mind unmoving, one attains fearlessness; Bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, Causing them to give rise to the unsurpassed bodhicitta, And reverently practicing until reaching the other shore.
At that time, the great bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
Thus concludes the *Sūtra on the Four Fearlessnesses* spoken by the Buddha.
